title: Viticulture in Depth
description: The vine's life cycle, site, soil, threats and farming philosophies, in the detail a professional needs.
L: Describe a vine's life from planting to old age
Explain why old vines are prized

A vine produces its first useful crop in its third or fourth year. It reaches full production around year 5 to 7 and can stay productive for 30 to 50 years. Older vines yield less but are often prized. Some vineyards, like in Barossa or parts of Spain, have vines over 100 years old.
First crop in year 3; full by 5 to 7

In the late 1800s phylloxera, a root-eating aphid from North America, destroyed most of Europe's vines. The solution was grafting European Vitis vinifera onto rootstocks of American species, whose roots resist the insect. Today almost all vineyards are grafted. Rootstocks are chosen for vigour, drought tolerance and soil type. Ungrafted vines survive in sandy soils and isolated places like Chile.
Why are most vines today grafted onto American rootstocks?
American species evolved with phylloxera and resist it. Grafting lets Vitis vinifera grow safely on top.

Old vines have deep roots and naturally low yields, so they often give concentrated, balanced fruit and cope better with drought. But there is no legal definition of old vines in most countries. South Africa's Old Vine Project certifies vines over 35 years old, and Barossa has a charter that grades old, survivor, centenarian and ancestor vines.
Ungrafted vines still grow in Chile.
Yes. Chile's isolation, protected by the Andes, the Pacific and the Atacama desert, has kept phylloxera out, so many vines grow on their own roots.
A vine crops from year 3 and can produce for decades
Grafting onto American rootstocks protects against phylloxera
Old vines give lower yields and often more concentrated fruit
How the shape of the year matters
Describe how climate change affects vineyards

Continentality describes the difference between the hottest and coldest months. Continental climates, far from the sea, have hot summers and cold winters, short seasons and frost risk, like Burgundy or Germany. Maritime climates, near oceans, have mild winters and cooler summers, with more rain, like Bordeaux. Mediterranean climates have warm, dry summers.

Diurnal range is the difference between day and night temperatures. A large range, common at altitude or in deserts, gives warm days for sugar and cool nights that slow the loss of acidity and keep aromas. Mendoza can see a 15 to 20 degree swing; Washington's Columbia Valley is similar.
Match each region to its climate.
Climate type shapes ripening and risk.

Average temperatures in many wine regions have risen by about 1 to 2 degrees since the 1980s. Harvests are earlier, sometimes by two or three weeks, alcohol levels higher and acidity lower. Growers respond with later-ripening grapes, higher sites, more shade and new regions, like southern England and Tasmania.
Earlier harvests, riper wines, new regions
Which are common effects of climate change in vineyards?
Heat raises sugar and lowers acidity. Hail, drought and fire have become more common.
Continental climates are extreme; maritime ones are mild and damp
A large diurnal range keeps acidity and aroma
Climate change brings earlier harvests and new regions
Explain how slopes and water reduce frost

Aspect is the direction a slope faces. In the northern hemisphere, south-facing slopes get the most sun, and south-east slopes catch the morning warmth. In the southern hemisphere it's the reverse. In cool regions like the Mosel, the right aspect can be the difference between ripe and unripe grapes.
Face the sun in cool regions

Cold air is heavier than warm air, so on still, clear nights it flows downhill and pools in valley floors. Slopes stay warmer and avoid spring frost. Growers fight frost with wind machines that mix in warmer air, heaters, or sprinklers that coat buds in ice, which releases heat as it freezes and holds them at about 0 degrees.
Cold air flows down; slopes escape frost
Why can sprinkling water on vines protect them from frost?
Freezing water releases heat, keeping buds near zero
As water freezes it releases latent heat, holding the bud at about 0 degrees and protecting it from colder temperatures.

Rivers and lakes store heat and release it slowly, moderating temperatures and reducing frost. They also reflect light onto slopes. The Mosel, the Rhine and the Douro all temper their valleys; Lake Geneva and the Finger Lakes in New York do the same. Mist from water can also help noble rot develop, as on the Ciron in Sauternes.
In the southern hemisphere, the warmest slopes face ____.
In the southern hemisphere the sun is to the north, so north-facing slopes get most light.
Aspect controls how much sun a slope receives
Cold air drains downhill; slopes escape frost
Rivers and lakes moderate temperature and reflect light
Explain how soil affects water and heat
Explain the main nutrients and vigour
Separate facts from myths about minerality

Soil texture controls water. Sand and gravel drain fast; clay holds water. Deep soils let roots explore. Stony surfaces radiate heat at night, as in Châteauneuf-du-Pape's galets. Dark soils absorb more heat; pale chalk reflects it. Drainage and water supply matter more for quality than chemistry.

Vines need nitrogen, potassium, phosphorus and trace elements. Too much nitrogen gives vigour: dense leaves shade the fruit, and ripening suffers. Too little stunts the vine and can cause stuck fermentations, because yeast also needs nitrogen. Growers balance this with cover crops, compost and careful fertilising.
Too much nitrogen: leaves over fruit
What problem can too much nitrogen cause in a vineyard?
Excess vigour that shades the fruit
High nitrogen pushes leaf and shoot growth, shading the fruit and slowing ripening.

Many tasters describe wines as mineral, saline or stony. But vines don't transfer the taste of rocks into the wine: minerals in wine are present in tiny amounts, far below what we can taste. The sensation probably comes from high acidity, low fruit intensity, reduction compounds and sometimes salt. Soil influences wine through water and heat, not by direct flavour.
Soil shapes wine through water, not taste
The flavour of slate in a Mosel Riesling comes directly from minerals absorbed by the vine.
Not true. Mineral levels in wine are far too low to taste. Slate influences the wine through heat and drainage, and the mineral sensation is likely linked to acidity and other compounds.
Soil matters mainly through water supply and heat
Nitrogen must be balanced: too much brings vigour, too little stresses yeast
Minerality is real as a sensation, but not a direct taste of rocks

Powdery mildew, or oidium, covers leaves and berries with grey powder; it likes warm, shady conditions. Downy mildew, or peronospora, spreads in warm, wet weather. Botrytis bunch rot ruins grapes in wet harvests. All three came, or spread, in the 19th century. Sulphur sprays control powdery mildew; copper sprays, like Bordeaux mixture, control downy mildew.

Phylloxera attacks roots; grafting is the defence. Insects like grape moths damage berries and open the door to rot. Birds and wild boar eat ripe grapes. Viruses, like leafroll, spread through cuttings and insects; they reduce yield and delay ripening, and the only cure is replanting with clean material. Trunk diseases slowly kill old vines.
Grafting for phylloxera; clean stock for viruses
Match each problem to its main control.
Each threat has its own defence.

Modern growers combine methods: canopy management for airflow, resistant rootstocks, weather-based spraying only when risk is high, and natural predators. Pheromone traps confuse grape moths so they can't mate. New disease-resistant varieties, called PIWI, are being planted to cut spraying.
Downy mildew needs warmth and moisture. Dry heat discourages it.
Powdery and downy mildew and botrytis are the main fungal threats
Grafting stops phylloxera; clean stock limits viruses
Integrated protection combines canopy work, timing and natural tools
Compare bush vines and trellised systems

Bush vines, or gobelet, stand alone without wires, shading their fruit; they suit hot, dry, windy places like southern Spain or Barossa's old vineyards. Trellised systems hold shoots along wires, giving even sun exposure and making mechanisation possible. Vertical shoot positioning, or VSP, is the most common trellis in cool regions.
Bush in heat; trellis for control

In winter, growers prune to decide how many buds, and so how many bunches, each vine carries. Cane pruning leaves one or two long canes of last year's wood, each with 8 to 15 buds; common in Bordeaux and New Zealand. Spur pruning leaves short spurs of 2 or 3 buds along a permanent arm, called a cordon; easier to mechanise.
Canes are long; spurs are short
Why are bush vines common in hot, dry regions?
Their leaves shade the fruit and they need no wires
They are easy to machine harvest
The open, low shape shades the grapes from harsh sun and suits poor, dry soils without the cost of trellising.

Canopy management balances leaves and fruit. About 1 to 1.5 m2 of leaf area per kilo of fruit ripens it well. In cool, damp places, growers remove leaves around bunches for sun and airflow. In hot ones, they keep leaves to prevent sunburn, or use shade netting. Hedging, topping and shoot thinning fine-tune the canopy.
Enough leaves to ripen, enough air to stay healthy
In very hot regions, growers often remove all leaves around the bunches to maximise sunlight.
Not true. In hot regions, exposed bunches can sunburn. Growers usually keep leaves for shade; leaf removal is more common in cool, damp places.
Bush vines suit heat and drought; trellises give control
Cane pruning keeps long canes; spur pruning short spurs
Canopy management balances sunlight, airflow and ripening

Organic viticulture bans synthetic fertilisers, herbicides and most synthetic pesticides. Copper and sulphur are allowed, though copper is limited in the EU to 28 kg per hectare over 7 years. In the EU, organic wine also has lower sulphite limits: 100 mg/l for dry reds compared with 150 mg/l for conventional ones. Conversion takes three years.

Biodynamics, based on Rudolf Steiner's 1924 lectures, goes further. The farm is treated as a self-sustaining organism. Growers use preparations, such as cow manure buried in a horn over winter, in tiny doses, and time work by a lunar and astrological calendar. Certification is by Demeter or Biodyvin. Scientific evidence for the preparations is limited, but many top producers follow it.
A farm as an organism, with preparations and a calendar
Match each term to its focus.
Each approach has its own rules and certifiers.

Sustainable programmes look at the whole business: water and energy use, biodiversity, workers' welfare and economic viability. They allow some synthetic inputs when justified. Examples include Sustainable Winegrowing New Zealand, the California Certified Sustainable Winegrowing programme and France's HVE, Haute Valeur Environnementale.
Which of these is allowed in organic viticulture?
Copper and sulphur are allowed in organic farming, with copper limited by law.
Organic bans synthetic chemicals and lowers sulphite limits
Biodynamics adds preparations and a calendar, with limited scientific evidence
Sustainable programmes cover environment, people and economics
Explain the vine's life and protection
What was the solution to phylloxera?
American rootstocks resist the root-eating aphid.
Match each site factor to its effect.
Site choice shapes ripening and risk.
Which are common responses to downy mildew?
Extra nitrogen would increase vigour and dampness, making disease worse.
Organic wines in the EU have lower maximum sulphite levels than conventional ones.
Yes. For dry reds, the limit is 100 mg/l instead of 150 mg/l.
Pruning that leaves short spurs of two or three buds is called ____ pruning.
Spur pruning leaves short spurs on a permanent arm. Cane pruning keeps long canes.
Grafting saves vines from phylloxera; old vines give concentration
Continentality, diurnal range and site shape ripening
Fungal diseases need sulphur, copper and good canopies
Organic, biodynamic and sustainable farming each set different rules
